key: That One Thing, breathless, breathed by its own nature: apart from it was nothing whatsoever.
s: In a hymn on the time when neither non-existent nor existent was, which asks whence creation came, the verse tells what alone there was; Sāyaṇa, on 10.129.2, takes the One as Brahman, known throughout the Vedānta, and ‘its own nature’ as māyā, undivided from it.

evidence.words: “तत्” सकलवेदान्तप्रसिद्धं ब्रह्मतत्त्वम् “आनीत्” प्राणितवत्। … स्वस्मिन् धीयते ध्रियत आश्रित्य वर्तत इति स्वधा माया। तया तद्ब्रह्मैकमविभागापन्नमासीत्।
evidence.gloss: ‘That’ is the reality of Brahman, well known throughout the Vedānta; ‘breathed’: it was as though breathing. … Svadhā (‘its own nature’) is what is placed and held in oneself, what exists resting on it: māyā. With it that Brahman was one, having come to be undivided.

reason: Second judgement with the refutation in hand: the refuter is right on both counts and the entry can be put right. Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, Rig Veda 10.129.2, at [965,2]). Opened packet.js veda 123 --verse 10.129.2 and 10.129.1: Sāyaṇa glosses tat as the reality of Brahman known throughout the Vedānta and svadhā as māyā, with which that Brahman was one, undivided (avibhāgāpannam); Wilson’s unbracketed note agrees he takes svadhā as Māyā. Reading holds. CHANGED: (1) the reading quoted six words of the key verse (‘That One Thing’, ‘its own nature’), over rule 3’s three; now only ‘its own nature’ is quoted and the first becomes the One. (2) The context clause said the hymn asks what was before existent and non-existent; 10.129.1 says neither then was, and 10.129.6 asks whence creation came, so the clause now says that. Entry-check ok.
